## Ordinary concepts: one file

Each Rust chapter has a \`~~~rust\` code block containing a complete \`fn main()\`. Copy it into a file and run \`rustc --edition 2024 main.rs && ./main\`.

The [curriculum checker](check_curriculum.py) compiles and executes each standalone chapter example with the pinned Rust toolchain in CI. They do not require Cargo dependencies or a runtime framework.

## Custom attribute macro: an honest exception

A custom attribute macro cannot be defined and used inside a single standard Rust source file. Rust requires a **separate crate of type \`proc-macro\`**. This project intentionally has only two tiny crates:

~~~text
examples/
  Cargo.toml
  attributes/
    Cargo.toml
    src/lib.rs       # defines #[add_label]
  app/
    Cargo.toml
    src/main.rs      # uses #[add_label]
~~~

Run from the repository root:

~~~bash
cargo +1.100.0 run --manifest-path programming-languages/rust/examples/Cargo.toml -p attribute-demo
cargo +1.100.0 test --manifest-path programming-languages/rust/examples/Cargo.toml --workspace
~~~

Expected output:

~~~text
hello: generated at compile time
~~~

### Three pieces of syntax to distinguish

1. **Attribute use:** \`#[derive(Debug)]\` invokes the standard Debug derive; it generates trait implementation code.
2. **Declarative macro definition:** \`macro_rules! twice { ... }\` defines a token-pattern macro invoked as \`twice!(value)\`.
3. **Custom attribute macro definition:** \`#[proc_macro_attribute]\` on a function in a special crate defines something you may invoke as \`#[add_label]\` in another crate.

The minimal \`add_label\` macro *keeps the annotated function* and appends a generated \`label()\` function. It does not manipulate syntax trees or reflect on runtime objects. It deliberately uses fixed output, so applying it twice in one module would create a name collision; real reusable macros need robust parsing, unique names, and good diagnostics.
